claims.text: Compositionally complex or high-entropy alloys can be used to produce a ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
Compositionally complex or high-entropy alloys are resistant to temper embrittlement.
Temper embrittlement occurs in conventional alloys within a narrow temperature window.
Temper embrittlement is absent in compositionally complex or high-entropy alloys.
Compositionally complex or high-entropy alloys possess unique atomic arrangements and interactions.
These unique atomic arrangements and interactions prevent a dramatic loss of ductility within a narrow temperature window.
Temperature variation will produce a ductile–brittle–ductile transition in compositionally complex or high-entropy alloys.
The predicted transition will occur without the significant loss of ductility observed in conventional alloys.
Observation of a significant, narrow-window loss of ductility comparable to conventional alloys would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The mediator and mechanism assert that a dramatic loss of ductility is absent or prevented, whereas the predicted ductile–brittle–ductile transition necessarily includes an intermediate brittle state. The hypothesis does not explain how brittleness arises without a substantial ductility loss.

Resistance to temper embrittlement is presented as the cause of a ductile–brittle–ductile transition, even though temper embrittlement would ordinarily be the phenomenon capable of generating the brittle portion of that transition.
